WORRY GUIDE — LIFE

When you're torn over taking a trip

You gaze at photos of places you'd like to visit, then close the tab. You look at the budget and put it off — it doesn't have to be now — and in the end, only the days off pass by. A travel plan has too many options: whether to go, where to go, what to do — none of it can all be decided at once. To be clear at the outset, most of being torn over travel comes not from having too many wishes, but from having no order. This page guides you through the order in which to decide.

POINT 01

What's making this hard

There are broadly three reasons you can't settle on travel. One is being torn over how to use money and time off. Is there another use for it? Is it all right to go while things are this busy? More than the trip itself, a sense of guilt makes the judgment heavy. The second is the sheer number of options. Destination, timing, lodging, travel companions. Try to optimize all of them at once, and none of them gets decided. The third is the expectation of a perfect trip. If you're going to go, you don't want it to fail. The stronger that feeling, the more research you do and the further the decision recedes. Once you can see what's making this hard, how you deal with it shifts from researching more to fixing the order in which you decide.

POINT 02

How to sort it out

The recommended order is purpose, schedule, budget, then destination. First, decide just one thing you most want from this trip. Is it rest, a break from the everyday, or time with someone? Once the purpose is one thing, the schedule and budget can be placed within a realistic range. The destination can come last. As long as a candidate fits the purpose, whichever you choose won't miss by much. This sorting goes more easily if you do it while drawing a card and looking at it. The card is not there to guess your destination; it is a mirror reflecting your current state — whether you are tired, or want stimulation. If you keep a record in a log of trips you took and trips you passed on, your next travel plan will come together surprisingly fast, because you can see your own travel preferences and patterns of regret.

POINT 03

How to read the cards

When you're torn over travel, cards that speak to outlook, movement, taking the plunge, juggling, and timing can offer useful clues.

The Three of Wands shows a figure gazing at the sea, waiting for a ship. It represents a state of having made a plan and waiting for the next step with an outlook in mind.

The Chariot is a young figure holding the reins and advancing by their own will. It points to the power to decide to go and start moving, and to movement itself.

The Fool shows someone stepping out lightly with a single bundle. It reminds you of the lightness at the start of a trip — leaping in without overthinking.

The Two of Pentacles is a figure handling two coins above the waves. It offers a perspective for balancing while juggling budget and schedule.

Wheel of Fortune shows a great wheel that keeps turning. It points to how timing comes around, and the judgment to ride the flow.

POINT 04

Questions to ask yourself

Try answering the following questions. What do you most want from this trip — rest, a break from the everyday, or time with someone? What schedule is available, and what is your budget ceiling, in concrete terms? If you narrowed your destination candidates to three, which would remain? If you didn't go, what would you likely use this time off for? If you narrowed the conditions a perfect trip needs to only those you truly can't give up, what would remain? Once your answers are together, all that is left is to decide. A small act of certainty — a booking — turns being torn into something to look forward to.

CARDS

Cards connected to this decision

  • Three of Wands

    A card that represents waiting for the next step with a plan and an outlook, in a figure gazing at the sea, waiting for a ship.

  • The Chariot

    A card that points to the power to decide to go and start moving, in a young figure advancing while holding the reins.

  • The Fool

    A card that reminds you of the start of a trip — leaping in without overthinking — in a figure stepping out lightly.

  • Two of Pentacles

    A card that represents a perspective for juggling budget and schedule, in a figure handling two coins.

  • Wheel of Fortune

    A card that points to how timing comes around and the judgment to ride the flow, in a wheel that keeps turning.

Go, or pass this time? Decide in order, starting from the purpose, and the travel plan moves forward. Why not sort it out through the questions the cards raise?
